issues.explanation: 'Object Throwing' is a weak fit as a trauma trigger for a life-threatening accident; it implies a violence/conflict cue rather than an accident-linked reminder, and it does not connect well to the rest of the profile's vehicle/safety themes.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Outsider: I am permanently an outsider now
issues.explanation: 'Outsider' is not impossible, but it sits awkwardly with the otherwise accident-focused profile and lacks a clear clinical bridge to the selected triggers, threat items, or coping responses; it reads more like an interpersonal/identity aftermath than the central formulation presented here.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: 'Inaction Guilt' is questionable for a life-threatening accident unless the patient had a clear preventable role. As selected, the rest of the profile does not support a responsibility-based narrative strongly enough to make this appraisal cohere.

issues.item: Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: 'Startle to Touch' is more suggestive of interpersonal assault-related threat than an accident-based threat pattern, and it is not well linked to the selected accident-relevant trigger/avoidance items.

issues.item: Undereating: I avoid eating or restrict food as a way of coping
issues.explanation: Undereating is hard to link coherently to the rest of the profile. The active formulation emphasizes a tight Triggers ↔ Threat ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop centered on accident-related cues and danger responses, but food restriction does not plausibly function as a strategy for the stated triggers or threats and is not supported elsewhere in the profile.

issues.item: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly
issues.explanation: Startle to unexpected touch points more toward interpersonal assault-related threat sensitivity than the otherwise accident-focused pattern. With the listed triggers centered on vehicles, illness, and loss of autonomy, this item is not impossible but is notably weakly connected to the rest of the threat profile and trauma type.

issues.item: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened
issues.explanation: Guilt about not doing more to stop what happened is difficult to reconcile with a life-threatening accident profile unless there is clear evidence of perceived preventability or responsibility. The rest of the appraisals emphasize helplessness and unfairness rather than responsibility, so this item pulls in a different direction and is hard to explain from the provided profile.

vignette:
Deborah is a 48-year-old social ministry worker who lives alone in a midwestern city. She came to therapy six months after a life-threatening accident that she still cannot fully describe without her voice dropping to a whisper. She had been driving home from a community outreach event late on a rainy November evening when a pickup truck ran a red light and T-boned her sedan at an intersection. The impact spun her car into a concrete median. She remembers the sound of metal crumpling, the smell of gasoline, and the terrifying realization that she could not move her legs for what felt like an eternity. Emergency crews had to cut her out of the vehicle. She was hospitalized for three days with a fractured pelvis and internal bruising, but physically she made a full recovery.

What stayed with Deborah, though, was not the pain of the injury but the feeling of absolute helplessness in those minutes after the crash. She had been pinned, unable to do anything, waiting for help that might not come. In the months since, she has come to believe that what happened to her was deeply unfair-and that nothing has been done about it. The other driver was never charged, and Deborah cannot shake the conviction that the world simply lets bad things happen without consequence. She finds herself thinking, "I can't stop bad things from happening to me," and this thought settles into her chest like a cold weight whenever she tries to go about her day.

The most disorienting change, however, is that Deborah no longer trusts her own body. Before the accident, she had been an active woman who walked to work and volunteered on weekends. Now, any sensation of physical strain-her heart beating faster after climbing stairs, her muscles aching after carrying groceries-sends a jolt of alarm through her. She has come to believe that her body is unreliable, that it might fail her at any moment. She avoids situations that put her body under stress, which means she no longer exercises, she takes the elevator even for one flight, and she has stopped helping with the heavy lifting at the church food pantry where she works.

Her work as a social ministry worker has become a minefield of triggers. She coordinates outreach programs, which used to involve driving to different neighborhoods to meet with families. Now she cannot drive at all. She cannot even be a passenger in a vehicle without her hands going clammy and her breath shortening. The sight of a car that has been in an accident-even a photograph in a news article-forces her to look away, her stomach clenching. She has arranged for colleagues to cover her driving duties, which has strained her relationships at work. They are understanding, but she can feel their patience thinning.

At home, Deborah has developed a pattern that puzzles even her. She avoids relaxing. Sitting on the couch with a cup of tea, letting her mind wander-these things feel dangerous, as though lowering her guard invites disaster. She keeps herself busy with small tasks until she is exhausted enough to sleep. When she does enter a room, she scans for exits immediately. At the grocery store, at church, at the doctor's office, she notes every door, every hallway. Even when a friend or coworker tells her she is safe, she finds it impossible to believe them. Ordinary sounds-a car horn outside, a door slamming, a dropped pan in the kitchen-make her jump as though she has been touched with electricity.

What finally brought Deborah to therapy was a panic episode at the food pantry last week. A volunteer dropped a metal tray, and Deborah screamed and backed into a corner, unable to breathe. She was mortified. She realized she cannot keep living this way, but she is also terrified that therapy will force her to relive the crash, or that she will never feel truly safe again. She hopes, quietly, that someone can help her trust her own body once more.
